messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Erik, a 45-year-old journalist, had been reporting from a conflict zone when a militia ambushed his convoy and took him prisoner. For six days he was held in a concrete room, blindfolded, his hands bound behind his back with a nylon cord that forced his head forward, putting a constant strain on his neck. His captors drank cheap rum throughout the day, the sour alcohol smell filling the space each time they leaned close to shove him or bark orders. He was released in a prisoner swap, but the terror did not end.

In the weeks that followed, the memory of the captivity returned as an unwelcome film that played without warning. The moment he tried to stretch his neck after a long day at his desk, the phantom ache of that forced posture would bloom, and with it the full sensory replay—the blindfold’s pressure, the rough hand on his shoulder, the rum-laced breath. He could be walking through the newsroom and suddenly catch the faintest whiff of liquor from a colleague’s coffee cup, and his throat would clench as though the room had shrunk to that cold concrete space. The memory did not simply visit; it brought the physical triggers along, a dark package that opened itself against his will.

His hypervigilance grew steadily. The clatter of a dropped keyboard, the slam of a filing cabinet, any unexpected sound sent him into a state of high alert. These startle responses soon began feeding the memories: a car backfiring in the street outside his home would throw him headlong into the image of the militia shouting, the cord digging into his wrists. The more he tried to stay watchful—scanning bar crowds for the shine of a bottle, turning his head at every sudden noise—the more the memory hijacked those moments. His constant readiness for danger also amplified the triggers themselves. When his wife touched his arm from behind, he flinched so hard she pulled back in hurt; the physical contact landed as a threat, not a gesture. A whiff of rum outside a restaurant was no longer a passing scent but an alert that set his heart racing. Hypervigilance made triggers feel inescapable because he was always scanning for them, and the scanning kept him raw.

At work, Erik began to avoid assignments that might take him near any hint of the conflict region. He turned down a profile on a foreign correspondent who had also been held captive, claiming scheduling conflicts. In the newsroom, he shifted his desk to a corner where fewer people walked behind him, and he asked colleagues not to tap his shoulder to get his attention—a request that felt reasonable to him but seemed puzzling to them. At home, he stopped drinking alcohol entirely; the smell had become unbearable, and even a wine cork’s aroma at a dinner party could send him into a cold sweat. His wife grew frustrated with his flinching and his tension, and their conversations became clipped.

The cycle tightened. He woke from nightmares with his neck screaming, and the pain itself triggered the memory again, which left him even more wired the next day. He reacted to false alarms repeatedly—once, he dove behind a parked car when a road crew’s jackhammer started—and each false alarm delivered another vivid replay of the captivity. By the time he sought help, he was exhausted, his marriage strained, and his professional reputation fraying from the assignments he had refused. What brought him to therapy was not the memories themselves but the growing certainty that he could not keep his life from shrinking any further. He was afraid that the next sound, the next touch, or the next stray smell would tighten the loop even more, and that he might lose everything he had built since returning home. He wanted to find a way to stop the film without first having to live through it again.
